note: Kona's tokens, and the only place any of them is decided.
This file exists because eight stylesheets each answered the same question
alone and disagreed: Kona's own orange was three different oranges
depending on which screen you were looking at (decision 3a). Every value
here is read off the mockups in design/mockups, which are the settled
design, and nothing below is a value somebody liked at the time.
Two rooms, because of decision 17: the panel is a dark slab, since it
floats over somebody else's article and has to stay legible over anything.
The library is your own room, and it is paper.
The boards were drawn by hand, so they hold twenty-four font sizes and
fourteen radii. What is below is a scale, and the rebuilt screens are
snapped to it rather than to the drawings pixel for pixel.
Generated from here: src/design/tokens.css, by scripts/tokens-css.mjs.
Read from here in TypeScript: src/design/tokens.ts. Run `npm run tokens`
after changing anything, or tests/designTokens.test.ts fails.
selectorNote: Three selectors, because the tokens have to land in two kinds of place.
:root is the web app and the extension's own pages. :host is the panel,
which lives in a shadow root with this stylesheet inlined into it, a
custom property on the page's :root would mean writing Kona's tokens into
somebody else's document, and the panel would then inherit whatever that
page had set. .kona-tokens is for anything mounted deeper than either.

groups.name: Pens
note: The four pens the palette starts with (decision 12).
Two values each. The dot is the pen at full strength, for Kona's own
rooms, where a colour sits on a plain background with nothing showing
through. The mark is what is painted over somebody's text, transparent
so the words underneath stay readable.
The mark alphas are not one number, on purpose: yellow is pale and
needs more of itself to register, green and pink are saturated and
need less before they swamp the text. The boards were drawn that way
and they are right.
A mark is transparent, so what the words end up sitting on is the
mark *and the page under it*. On a light page the dark ink reads at
9.5:1 or better; on a dark page the same ink lands on a dark
composite and falls to 1.5:1, which is a highlight that makes text
harder to read than not highlighting it. So there are two inks, and
the painter picks by how dark the page is. Measured worst pen: 9.52
with the dark ink on white, 5.02 with the light ink on near-black.
A mid-grey page is the one neither can fix, and the light ink is the
better of the two there.
The boards paint the in-page mark as a vertical gradient. The CSS
Custom Highlight API cannot render one: ::highlight() takes a flat
background-color and little else, so each mark is the flat value at
the middle of the gradient it was drawn as.

groups.name: Accent
note: Kona's colour, once. This is the value that was three values.
The link is a darker orange than the accent because it is text on
paper and has to be readable as text; the accent is for a shape.
The fill is a third value, and it exists because the accent as a
*background* is a different problem from the accent as a line or a
word. Measured: white on #ea580c is 3.50:1, which fails AA for normal
text; on #c2410c it is 5.09:1, which passes. Any button, chip or badge
that puts text *on* the accent uses the fill and its ink, not the
accent itself.
This was known once and then lost: it was a comment in the stylesheet
the rebuild deleted, and three filled buttons went out at 3.50:1
before it was noticed again. It is a token now so that it cannot be.

groups.name: Paper
note: The library, and every room of Kona's own. Light, because it is not
sitting on top of anybody else's page (decision 17).
The ink runs from a passage read back as prose, which is the darkest,
out to the uppercase labels, which are the faintest thing that is
still text.

groups.name: Slab
note: The panel in the page. Dark, and the same dark over a white article
or a black one, which is the whole reason it does not follow the
page's theme.
The going-to strip is its own small set because it is the one thing
the panel must always be able to say (decision 2e), and it is drawn
in the accent so it cannot be mistaken for the page.
The ink has six steps because the boards use six, and the bar is what
needs the last two: a control's label sits above the chip grey, and
Delete is the one warm one, because it is the only thing on the bar
that cannot be undone by doing it again.

groups.name: Type
note: Two families. The interface is Inter, and a passage read back as
prose is Source Serif 4, which is what the boards draw in the
library.
Neither is fetched. Decision 6 forbids anything being fetched because
of a page you are reading, and a webfont in the panel would be a
request to Google on every page you read. The files are bundled; the
stacks below are what shows until they are.
The sizes are a scale, not the drawings. The boards use 12.5 and 13
half a pixel apart in the same panel, and a scale has to collapse
that or it is a list.

groups.name: Space
note: Named by size rather than by step number, so that reading a rule
tells you roughly how big the gap is without counting.

groups.name: Radius
note: The mark on the text is the smallest, because it wraps a few words
and anything rounder reads as a button. The pill is for a chip.

groups.name: Shadow
note: Only the things that float have one: the panel, and the small mark
it rests as. Everything in the library sits on paper and is
separated by a line instead.

darkNote: Dark, for the rooms that are made of paper.
Settings offered Match the system, Light and Dark from the day it was
written, and stamped the answer on <html> as data-theme. Nothing read
it. There was no dark anywhere in this file, so the choice moved a
value nothing was looking at and the library stayed cream whichever
chip was lit. A control that does nothing is worse than no control: it
tells somebody their eyes are wrong rather than the product.
**Only paper goes dark, and only at the document.** The slab tokens
below are the panel in the page, which 17 settled as dark over a white
article and dark over a black one, so it is the one surface that must
not follow anybody's preference. That is why these are emitted against
:root alone and never against :host or .kona-tokens: the panel is
drawn inside a shadow root wearing that class, and a rule that reached
it would undo the decision by accident.
The pens are not here either. A mark is a transparent wash over
somebody else's words, and the painter already picks its ink by how
dark the page is rather than by what the reader prefers.
Contrast measured against the dark paper: ink 16.0, headings 17.2,
muted 6.7, the link 10.9. The faint tone lands at 4.2, which is above
where the light theme puts the same token, at 3.4.
